## TL;DR

Implemented automatic recovery for two idle-task failure modes. Review-agent failures that produce no usable report are retried up to the configured `review.failedReportRetries` bound, then surfaced as `needs_input` with an explicit reason. An overdue queued engineer message can restart an engineer when no engineer is live, using the configured `watchdog.queuedMessageRecoverMs` threshold. Both paths exclude held, paused, and human-assigned tasks; queue recovery also retains the pressure-guard and worktree safety checks. Settings controls, docs, and regression coverage are included.

## Work and rationale

I began by tracing the review pipeline and watchdog/recovery paths called out in the task. The failed-review retry mechanism was already partly present in the review flow, including a configurable retry count and activity logging. I completed the missing safety behavior around it: a shared predicate now prevents automatic recovery for archived, human-owned, held, or paused tasks, and the retry timer checks that predicate again before it starts work. Rechecking at the timer boundary matters because task ownership or hold state can change after the failure has been recorded.

For queued engineer messages, the watchdog now passes the configured recovery interval into the existing active-without-engineer recovery path. When a queued message exceeds that interval and there is no live engineer, the recovery path can shorten its usual idle window and restart the engineer on the existing task worktree. Its activity entry explains that an overdue queued message triggered the restart. Existing start and worktree orchestration remains responsible for pressure-guard admission and process handoff; I did not add a path that bypasses those controls. The watchdog’s queued-message recovery filter now explicitly handles both human assignment field forms, as well as held and paused states.

I kept the behavior configurable through the existing watchdog and review configuration sections. The schema, supported-key/parser coverage, and Settings controls are tested. The queued-message setting description now explains that it covers an absent engineer as well as a live silent turn. I updated the agent run-operations documentation and user configuration guide to describe the retry bound, restart threshold, exclusions, and resulting task state.

Tests cover the configurable controls and the key state boundaries: held, paused, and human-owned tasks do not enter either recovery path; overdue queued messages do recover otherwise eligible tasks; and the Settings page renders both numeric controls. The existing manual “Review again” test also sets automatic failed-report retries to zero, so it continues to test the human retry action deterministically after automatic retries were introduced.

## Approaches tried

I first ran the prescribed changed-path check locally. Early attempts showed formatting issues, which I corrected with the repository formatter. Subsequent local full-suite attempts encountered load-sensitive timeouts while the RepoOS pressure guard reported high load. I isolated the first remote-host lock timeouts and confirmed those tests passed by themselves. I then used the normal RepoOS check again, allowing its remote validation runner to execute the tests. The first remote run passed the full test suite but exposed a worktree-drift guard failure because the manual Review again test needed explicit retry configuration. I retained that related regression-test adjustment and reran the complete check. The final run passed all 545 test files, the build and lint/format steps, rendered contrast, UI smoke, and user-docs build.

## Challenges and blockers

The main challenge was distinguishing code regressions from test failures caused by contention. The local host was under enough load to trigger the project’s pressure guard and stretch subprocess timing tests. I followed the guard’s reported state and used remote validation rather than weakening timeouts or changing test concurrency. The temporary drift failure also highlighted that enabling automatic recovery changes the assumptions of an existing manual-retry test; making that test’s configuration explicit preserves its original purpose.

No implementation blocker remains. The final check completed successfully, including RepoOS’s worktree-drift validation.

## Key learnings

A retry timer is a second decision point: it must re-evaluate whether recovery is still allowed, rather than trusting eligibility from the failure event. Automatic activity should name the concrete trigger, because a task that remains in review or `needs_input` otherwise hides whether anyone is expected to act. Finally, an existing manual recovery test should opt out of the newly introduced automation when its purpose is to verify the manual action itself.
